Haiku. A traditional Japanese poetic form consisting of three lines following a five-seven-five syllable pattern, typically focusing on nature, seasons, and moments of insight or beauty. Emerging in the sixteenth century and refined into an art form by masters like Matsuo Bashō in the seventeenth century, haiku embodies Zen Buddhist aesthetics and has become one of the world's most recognized and imitated poetic forms.

The form adheres strictly to five-seven-five syllable counts across its three lines, creating a compressed structure that demands precision and economy of language. Matsuo Bashō, living from sixteen forty-four to sixteen ninety-four, elevated haiku from a parlor game into serious literary art, and his works exemplify the form's aesthetic ideals: simplicity, nature imagery, and moments of spiritual insight. Haiku traditionally incorporates a kigo, a seasonal reference, and a kireji, a cutting word—poetic devices that ground the poem in seasonal time and create sharp juxtaposition or insight, though these elements are debated in modern haiku practice.

The form reflects Zen Buddhist influence through emphasis on direct observation of nature, the beauty of impermanence, and sudden enlightenment, called satori, conveyed through precise, minimal language. Common haiku themes include landscapes, wildlife, weather, seasons, and transient moments, with many haiku juxtaposing two images to create metaphorical meaning through contrast. The form was initially called hokku, meaning opening verse, and was part of renga, linked-verse poetry, where multiple poets contributed stanzas in succession. Over time it became a standalone form. Haiku spread globally in the twentieth century, influencing American and European poets and being adopted by Modernists through the Imagist movement. It has been adapted into dozens of languages, though debates persist about how to preserve the form outside Japanese contexts.
